title: La Liga Chief Tebas Calls on FIFA's Infantino to Resign Over World Cup Overreach
excerpt: Spain's top football administrator accuses FIFA of 'destroying the football industry' through relentless tournament expansion and political interference, joining a growing chorus demanding change at the governing body.
body:
• La Liga president Javier Tebas has called on FIFA president Gianni Infantino to resign, accusing the governing body of destroying the football industry through tournament expansion.
  • Tebas slammed plans to expand the World Cup to 64 teams, warning that domestic leagues and tens of thousands of jobs are at risk from international fixture overload.
  • The La Liga chief called FIFA's suspension of Folarin Balogun's red card ban — following Donald Trump's intervention — a matter of "absolute gravity."
  • Despite growing criticism from UEFA, former FIFA president Sepp Blatter, and league executives, Infantino retains backing from over 200 of FIFA's 211 member federations ahead of his March 2027 re-election bid.

La Liga president Javier Tebas has declared that FIFA president Gianni Infantino's "time is up," becoming the most senior league executive to publicly call for the Swiss administrator's resignation in the wake of a controversy-laden 2026 World Cup.

In an interview with Italian newspaper La Gazzetta dello Sport, reported by Reuters, Tebas accused FIFA of "destroying the football industry" by prioritizing its own revenue-generating international competitions over domestic leagues and clubs that form the backbone of professional football.

"In my opinion, yes, I think his time is up. He shouldn't stay, but the current state of affairs means he won't leave."

— Javier Tebas, La Liga President

A System 'Flawed From the Ground Up'

Tebas's broadside comes as FIFA faces a reckoning after the first-ever 48-team World Cup drew both record attendance — 65,351 per match with stadiums 99.7 percent full, according to FIFA figures — and a parade of governance controversies across the month-long tournament in the United States, Canada and Mexico.

The La Liga chief directed particular fire at proposals to expand the World Cup further to 64 teams for the 2030 edition, set to be co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with opening matches in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay.

"Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense," Tebas told La Gazzetta dello Sport. "The football industry isn't just the World Cup. It's the national competitions that sustain this sport."

He argued that FIFA's expansion agenda threatens the livelihoods of workers across European football. "They're destroying the football industry, the one that generates tens of thousands of jobs — for an event that lasts 40 days and only a minority of players attend," he said.

The Balogun Affair and Political Interference

Tebas reserved his sharpest criticism for FIFA's handling of the Folarin Balogun red card controversy, which dominated headlines during the tournament. The U.S. striker was sent off against Bosnia-Herzegovina but had his automatic one-match ban suspended by FIFA's disciplinary committee after U.S. President Donald Trump personally called Infantino to discuss the case.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=b_SOUATNqTY

The decision, which allowed Balogun to play in the U.S.'s Round of 16 match against Belgium — a game the Americans lost 4-1 — drew a furious response from UEFA, which said the decision "crossed a red line." UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin boycotted the World Cup final in protest, according to sources cited by The Times.

"The suspension of the American player's disqualification is something of absolute gravity," Tebas said. "They were lucky Belgium eliminated the USA because otherwise a case could have been created that could have cost Infantino his job."

Blatter and Broader Backlash

Tebas is far from alone in his criticism. Former FIFA president Sepp Blatter, whom Infantino replaced in 2016 on a platform of cleaning up the organization, called his successor "a dictator," according to talkSPORT. Nathan Goldberg Crenier, vice-president of U.S. Soccer, wrote in The Guardian that Infantino's leadership reflects "a battle for the soul of the sport."

The Council of Europe has urged FIFA to implement a robust governance framework ahead of the 2030 tournament, warning of a potential "crisis" if political interference and commercialization continue unchecked.

Tebas also dismissed the widely criticized hydration breaks during the World Cup as advertising breaks in disguise. "In LaLiga we have them, but only when it's really hot. In Dallas, Los Angeles, or Atlanta, there was air conditioning. It was a lie: a break for advertising," he said. UEFA has confirmed it will not use the format in its competitions.

India's Football Aspirations and the FIFA Question

For India's football community, the power struggle at the top of world football carries real implications. The All India Football Federation (AIFF) is one of FIFA's 211 member associations whose vote will shape the organization's direction at the March 2027 congress in Morocco. India's ambitions to qualify for a men's World Cup — a long-standing goal for a country with one of the world's largest football fan bases — depend partly on whether FIFA continues expanding tournaments or redirects resources toward developing the sport at the grassroots level in emerging markets.

What Happens Next

Despite the mounting criticism, Infantino's position appears secure. He announced in April that he will seek a fourth term, and has already secured endorsement letters from more than 200 FIFA member associations. The presidential vote is scheduled for March 18, 2027, in Morocco.

Tebas acknowledged the structural challenge facing any potential opposition. "There's no opposition candidate; no one wants to run to lose," he said. "This is the system, and it's a system that's flawed from the ground up."

Yet cracks are showing. Germany, Spain and Norway are among the federations that have not endorsed Infantino, and there are growing calls from within UEFA to field a rival candidate — even if only to force a public debate. The November 18 deadline for candidates to enter the race leaves a window for a challenger to emerge, though any upset would require, as The Guardian put it, "a political earthquake."
